mainTopic: Health and modesty, דוד's census and plague, and respect for הר הבית and the בית הכנסת (ברכות סב:)
overview: This amud first collects practical advice about the body and about modesty. It opens with health tips from בן עזאי, שמואל and בר קפרא, then אביי's warning to keep your eyes down on the paths of מחוזא. Next come stories about the בית הכסא. רבי אבא rebukes רב ספרא for speaking from inside it, and the גמרא defends רב ספרא because holding oneself back is dangerous. A Roman who pushed רבי אלעזר out of a בית הכסא dies in his place. The גמרא then shows how שאול's צניעות in the cave saved his life from דוד. That leads into stories about דוד: he cut שאול's robe, he called ה׳ a 'מסית', and he counted ישראל without a כופר, which brought a plague that ended with the death of אבישי בן צרויה. Several אמוראים discuss what ה׳ 'saw' to stop the plague, and the גמרא concludes it was the בית המקדש. Finally the גמרא returns to the משנה's laws of respect for הר הבית: making it a shortcut (קפנדריא), when a shortcut through a בית הכנסת is allowed, and spitting. רבא rules that spitting is allowed in a בית הכנסת, and his challenger presses him to be strict in both places; רבא's reply comes on the next amud.

steps.title: בן עזאי: where to lie and where to sit
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes בן עזאי: you may lie on any bed except the bare ground, and sit on any seat except a narrow beam.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: בן עזאי says: Lie down on any bed except the ground. Sit on any seat except a beam.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with health and safety advice from בן עזאי about lying down and sitting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Lying on the bare ground is bad for your health. Sitting on a narrow beam is risky because you could fall off. This is practical life advice, not a legal ruling about איסור and היתר.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא (a teaching from the time of the תנאים that is not in the משנה)
A bed, a place to lie down

phrases.english: It was taught in a baraita: Ben Azzai says:
On any bed, lie down,
except for the ground.
phrases.notes: Lying on the bare ground is unhealthy.

phrases.english: On any seat, sit,
except for a beam.
phrases.notes: Because you might fall off.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier part of the daf, which collects health and behavior advice.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Lie anywhere except the bare ground. Sit anywhere except a narrow beam.

steps.title: שמואל: sleep and relieving oneself at dawn strengthen the body
steps.stepSummary: שמואל says that sleeping at dawn and relieving oneself at dawn strengthen the body the way forging strengthens iron.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: Sleep at dawn is like tempering for iron. Relieving oneself at dawn is like tempering for iron.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל adds two more health tips. Both are about the early morning, and both use the same comparison.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When iron is heated and hammered, it becomes strong. שמואל says that sleep and relieving oneself at עמוד השחר do the same for the body. The repeated wording shows these are two separate pieces of advice.

keyTerms.meaning: Dawn, the first light of morning

phrases.english: Shmuel said:
Sleep at dawn
is like tempering to iron.
Relieving oneself at dawn
is like tempering to iron.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds more health advice after בן עזאי's.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sleeping and relieving oneself at dawn strengthen the body.

steps.title: בר קפרא's sayings: don't delay what your body needs
steps.stepSummary: בר קפרא taught short, valuable sayings: eat when hungry, drink when thirsty, and relieve yourself while the urge is there.
steps.simpleTranslation: בר קפרא would sell sayings for דינרים: While you are hungry, eat. While you are thirsty, drink. While your pot is boiling, pour it out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings short sayings of בר קפרא. They tell you not to delay the body's needs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His sayings were so valuable it was as if he sold them for gold coins. If you wait too long, the hunger or thirst passes and the food no longer helps you. 'Pouring the boiling pot' is a polite image for relieving yourself right away, which fits this daf's topic of the בית הכסא.
steps.confusionAlert: The 'boiling pot' is not about cooking. It is a polite way to say: relieve yourself as soon as you need to, and don't hold it in.

phrases.aramaic: בַּר קַפָּרָא הֲוָה מְזַבֵּן מִילֵּי בְּדִינָרֵי:
phrases.english: Bar Kappara would sell sayings for dinars:
phrases.notes: His short sayings were worth a lot.

phrases.english: While you are hungry, eat.
While you are thirsty, drink,
while your pot is boiling, pour it out.
phrases.notes: He means: when you need to relieve yourself, go right away and don't hold it in.

steps.triggerLanguage: בַּר קַפָּרָא הֲוָה מְזַבֵּן מִילֵּי בְּדִינָרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues with advice about the body's needs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Don't delay eating, drinking, or relieving yourself.

steps.title: בר קפרא: seize the opportunity when it comes
steps.stepSummary: Another saying of בר קפרא: when the market in רומי calls for figs, the fig seller's son should sell his father's figs right away.
steps.simpleTranslation: When the horn sounds in רומי, son of a fig seller, sell your father's figs.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings one more saying of בר קפרא, with the same idea: act at the right moment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The horn in רומי announces that figs are in demand. The son should sell even without asking his father first, so the chance is not lost. Opportunities don't wait, just as the body's needs don't wait.

phrases.english: When the horn sounds in Rome,
phrases.notes: A signal that figs are in demand.

phrases.english: son of a fig seller,
sell your father's figs.
phrases.notes: Even without his permission, so the opportunity is not missed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second saying of the same speaker, with a similar message.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Grab a good opportunity the moment it comes.

steps.title: אביי: keep your eyes down on the paths of מחוזא
steps.stepSummary: אביי tells the רבנן that when they walk the paths of מחוזא to relieve themselves in the field, they should not look to either side.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to the רבנן: When you enter the paths of מחוזא to go out to the field, do not look to this side or that side. Women may be sitting there, and it is not דרך ארץ to look at them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves from health tips to modesty. אביי gives the רבנן a rule about where to look.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People went out to the fields to relieve themselves. Women might also be sitting there for the same reason. Looking at them would be immodest, so the רבנן should keep their eyes straight ahead.

phrases.english: Abaye said to the Sages:
When you enter the paths of Meḥoza
to go out to relieve yourselves in the field,
do not look, not to this side
and not to that side,
since perhaps women are sitting there,
and it is not proper conduct to look at them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from health advice to modesty when going out to relieve oneself.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: On the way to relieve yourself in the field, don't look to the sides, because looking at women is not דרך ארץ.

steps.title: The story: רב ספרא answers from inside the בית הכסא
steps.stepSummary: רב ספרא was in the בית הכסא. רבי אבא coughed at the door to check if it was free, and רב ספרא called out, 'Let the master enter.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ספרא went into the בית הכסא. רבי אבא came and coughed at the door. רב ספרא said to him: Let the master come in.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story. This step sets up the scene for רבי אבא's criticism in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אבא coughed to find out if someone was inside. רב ספרא answered with words, inviting him in. That spoken answer from inside the בית הכסא is what רבי אבא will object to.

phrases.english: Rav Safra entered the bathroom.
Rabbi Abba came,
and coughed at the door.
phrases.notes: To check whether someone was inside.

phrases.english: He (Rav Safra) said to him: Let the master enter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of modesty and דרך ארץ around relieving oneself, now through a story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The story's facts: רב ספרא spoke from inside the בית הכסא.

steps.title: רבי אבא's rebuke: you learned the ways of שעיר
steps.stepSummary: After רב ספרא came out, רבי אבא criticized him for speaking from the בית הכסא, calling it the behavior of שעיר.
steps.simpleTranslation: After he came out, רבי אבא said to him: Until now you never went to שעיר, and already you learned the ways of שעיר!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבא challenges what רב ספרא did. He says that speaking from inside the בית הכסא is immodest behavior.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שעיר is the land of אדום, which was known for not being careful about modesty. רבי אבא's point is that רב ספרא should have stayed silent. He will now support this with a source.

phrases.english: After he came out, he (Rabbi Abba) said to him:
Until now you have not entered Seir,
and you have already learned the ways of Seir!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reacts critically to רב ספרא's spoken answer in the previous step.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ספרא's behavior of speaking from inside the בית הכסא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Speaking from the בית הכסא is immodest, like the ways of שעיר, so רב ספרא should not have done it.

steps.title: Proof from the משנה about the honorable בית הכסא in the בית המקדש
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא cites a משנה about the בית המקדש: its בית הכסא was 'honorable' because people could tell whether it was occupied just by whether it was locked or open, with no need to speak.
steps.simpleTranslation: Didn't we learn this in a משנה: There was a fire there and an honorable בית הכסא. Its honor was this: if one found it locked, it was known someone was inside. If one found it open, it was known no one was inside.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבא brings a source to back up his rebuke. The משנה describes how people knew if the בית הכסא in the בית המקדש was in use.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה calls that בית הכסא 'honorable' because a locked or open door told you everything. Nobody had to call out or answer. This shows that the honorable way is to avoid speaking there at all.

keyTerms.meaning: Didn't we learn this in a משנה?
A fire (for the כהנים to warm themselves)

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the practice of checking whether a bathroom is in use by looking or knocking, instead of talking back and forth.

phrases.english: Didn't we learn this in a mishna:
There was a fire there
phrases.notes: In the בית המקדש, near the place of immersion (משנה תמיד).

phrases.english: and an honorable bathroom.
And this was its honor:

phrases.aramaic: מְצָאוֹ נָעוּל — בְּיָדוּעַ שֶׁיֵּשׁ שָׁם אָדָם,
phrases.english: If one found it locked, it was known that someone was there;

phrases.aramaic: מְצָאוֹ פָּתוּחַ — בְּיָדוּעַ שֶׁאֵין שָׁם אָדָם.
phrases.english: if one found it open, it was known that no one was there.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבי אבא's rebuke with a source from a משנה.
steps.raayaObject: That speaking from inside the בית הכסא is not proper.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה about the honorable בית הכסא in the בית המקדש, where a locked or open door replaced speaking.

steps.title: Conclusion: speaking from the bathroom is not proper conduct
steps.stepSummary: From the משנה, רבי אבא concludes that speaking from the בית הכסא is not דרך ארץ.
steps.simpleTranslation: This shows that it is not proper conduct!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבא draws his conclusion from the משנה he just quoted, which closes the story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the 'honorable' arrangement was one where nobody needed to speak, then speaking there is the opposite of honorable. So רב ספרא's 'Let the master enter' was not proper.
steps.whatToRemember: Modesty around the בית הכסא includes not talking from inside it. Let a closed or open door, or a quiet signal, do the communicating. This continues אביי's theme of דרך ארץ in private matters.

phrases.english: This shows that it is not proper conduct!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the lesson from the משנה just quoted.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Speaking from inside the בית הכסא is not דרך ארץ.

steps.title: Why רב ספרא spoke anyway
steps.stepSummary: רב ספרא spoke from the בית הכסא because he held that making רבי אבא wait was dangerous.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he (רב ספרא) held that it is dangerous.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב ספרא against רבי אבא's criticism. רב ספרא knew speaking there is not דרך ארץ, but he thought making רבי אבא wait outside could harm his health.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אבא proved from the משנה that speaking in the בית הכסא is not proper. The גמרא does not reject that rule. It says danger to health outweighs this matter of manners, so רב ספרא spoke to let רבי אבא in quickly.

keyTerms.meaning: he held / was of the opinion

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying רבי אבא was wrong about the rule. It is explaining that רב ספרא had a special reason, danger, that overrode it.

phrases.english: But he (רב ספרא) held that it is dangerous.
phrases.notes: Waiting and holding oneself back can cause illness.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends רב ספרא against רבי אבא's conclusion in step 9
steps.terutzResolutionType: Overriding concern: danger to health outweighs manners
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב ספרא simply broke the rule of דרך ארץ
steps.terutzMaskana: He spoke on purpose to prevent danger to רבי אבא

steps.title: Proof that holding back causes illness
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says that holding back stool or urine causes disease.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: A held-back column of stool brings a person to dropsy. A held-back stream of urine brings a person to jaundice.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to prove that waiting really is dangerous.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Holding back stool causes הדרוקן (swelling of the body), and holding back urine causes ירקון (jaundice). This shows that רב ספרא's worry was a real medical danger, so speaking was justified.

keyTerms.meaning: as it was taught in a ברייתא
a 'column' of stool that is held back
a stream of urine that is held back

steps.whatToRemember: Holding oneself back from relieving oneself is treated as a real danger, and that danger can override normal rules of manners.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a source for the idea that one should not delay relieving oneself because of the health risk.

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא, רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: As it was taught: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
A column (of stool) that is held back
brings a person to dropsy.
A stream (of urine) that is held back
brings a person to jaundice.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the claim in step 10 that waiting is dangerous
steps.raayaSupportSource: ברייתא of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל

steps.title: A Roman pushes רבי אלעזר out and is killed
steps.stepSummary: A Roman pushed רבי אלעזר away from the בית הכסא, and a serpent killed the Roman.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר went into a בית הכסא. A certain Roman came and pushed him. רבי אלעזר got up and left. A serpent came and tore out the Roman's intestines.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a new story about the בית הכסא. A Roman rudely pushed רבי אלעזר away, and was then killed there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר did not fight back. He simply left. The Roman was punished in the very place where he had shamed the חכם.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar entered a bathroom.
A certain Roman came and pushed him.
Rabbi Elazar stood up and left.
A serpent came and tore out his (the Roman's) intestines.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: New story continuing the theme of conduct in the בית הכסא
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The Roman who pushed רבי אלעזר away was struck down in the בית הכסא

steps.title: רבי אלעזר applies a פסוק to the Roman
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר reads 'אדם' in ישעיהו as 'אדום', meaning Rome would be given in his place.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר read this verse about him: 'And I will give a man (אדם) in your place.' Do not read 'אדם' but 'אדום'.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר explains the event with a פסוק. ה׳ gave the Roman's life in place of his own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The serpent may have been waiting in the בית הכסא, so by pushing רבי אלעזר out, the Roman took the danger instead of him. By reading 'אדם' as 'אדום' (Rome), the פסוק describes exactly this: a Roman was given in his place.

keyTerms.meaning: do not read (it as)... a style of homiletic re-reading
Edom, a name used for Rome

steps.confusionAlert: 'אל תקרי' does not change the text of the פסוק. It is a דרשה that adds an extra layer of meaning.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar read about him:
"And I will give a man in your place" (Isaiah 43:4);
do not read 'adam' (man) but 'Edom' (Rome).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives scriptural meaning to the story in step 12
steps.raayaObject: That the Roman died in רבי אלעזר's place

steps.title: דוד's words to שאול in the cave
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes דוד's words to שאול: 'And he said to kill you, and it spared you.'
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And he said to kill you, and it spared you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a פסוק from when דוד found שאול relieving himself in the cave and spared him. This sets up the question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שאול went into the cave to relieve himself, and דוד secretly cut the corner of his coat. The wording 'he said' and 'it spared' sounds strange, because דוד is speaking about himself.

phrases.english: "And he said to kill you, and it spared you" (I Samuel 24:10).
phrases.notes: דוד speaking to שאול after the cave incident.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: New source on modesty in relieving oneself
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Base פסוק for the upcoming question

steps.title: The verse should have said 'I said' and 'I spared'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out the wording is odd: דוד should have said 'I said' and 'I spared'.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And he said'? It should say 'And I said'! 'And it spared'? It should say 'And I spared'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the wording of the פסוק. דוד is talking about himself, so why does he speak in the third person?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If דוד meant 'I thought of killing you but I spared you,' he would use first-person words. The odd wording hints that someone or something else is the one that 'said' and 'spared'.

phrases.english: 'And he said'? It should have said 'And I said'!
'And it spared'? It should have said 'And I spared'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the wording of the פסוק in step 14
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: דוד speaks about his own actions, so the verbs should be first person

steps.title: The Torah said to kill שאול, but his modesty saved him
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר explains: the Torah says a רודף may be killed, but שאול's צניעות spared him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: דוד said to שאול: By Torah law you deserve to be killed, because you are a pursuer, and the Torah said: If someone comes to kill you, rise early and kill him first. But the modesty you had is what spared you.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר answers the question. The one who 'said' to kill is the Torah, and the one who 'spared' is שאול's own modesty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'ואמר' means the Torah said: kill a רודף first, and שאול was chasing דוד to kill him. 'ותחס' means שאול's צניעות, how modestly he covered himself in the cave, is what spared him. That explains the third-person wording and teaches how great modesty in the בית הכסא is.

keyTerms.meaning: one who deserves to be killed
a pursuer who is trying to kill someone
rise early and kill him first

steps.whatToRemember: Modesty when relieving oneself is so valuable that it saved שאול's life, even though by Torah law he could have been killed as a רודף.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how much weight modest conduct in the בית הכסא carries, and it cites the famous rule of הבא להרגך השכם להרגו. The next steps spell out what שאול's צניעות actually was.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:
David said to Saul:
By Torah law you deserve to be killed,
since you are a pursuer,
and the Torah said:
phrases.notes: This is the 'he said' (ואמר) of the פסוק.

phrases.english: If one comes to kill you, rise early and kill him first,
but the modesty that was in you,
it is what spared you.
phrases.notes: This is the 'it spared' (ותחס) of the פסוק.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording question of step 15
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of the subjects of the verbs
steps.terutzHavaAmina: דוד was describing his own thoughts and mercy
steps.terutzMaskana: The Torah 'said' to kill שאול, and his modesty 'spared' him

steps.title: What was שאול's modesty?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what exactly the צניעות was that saved שאול.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is it (this modesty)?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question to set up the next move: what did שאול actually do that counted as צניעות? The answer comes in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 16, רבי אלעזר said שאול's צניעות spared him from being killed as a רודף. Now the גמרא wants the specific details behind that claim.

phrases.english: And what is it?
phrases.notes: Refers to שאול's modesty mentioned in step 16.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the details of the צניעות that step 16 referred to.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The specific act of צניעות that שאול did.

steps.title: The verse about שאול entering the cave
steps.stepSummary: The answer starts with the פסוק describing שאול going into a cave to relieve himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'And he came to the sheep-pens by the road, and there was a cave, and שאול went in to cover his feet.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by quoting the פסוק from שמואל א. It tells how שאול went into a cave to relieve himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'לְהָסֵךְ אֶת רַגְלָיו' (to cover his feet) is a polite way of saying he went to relieve himself. The next two steps take details from this פסוק to show how private he was.

keyTerms.meaning: 'To cover his feet', a polite phrase for relieving oneself

phrases.english: As it is written: 'And he came to the sheep-pens'
by the road, and there was a cave
and Saul went in to cover his feet.'
phrases.notes: שמואל א כד:ג

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question by bringing the source פסוק.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק about שאול entering the cave to relieve himself.

steps.title: A fence within a fence, a cave within a cave
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא explains that שאול went very deep inside for privacy, past fence after fence and cave after cave.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: there was a fence inside a fence, and a cave inside a cave, to relieve himself.
steps.whatsHappening: A ברייתא reads the פסוק as showing that שאול went deep into layers of enclosures just to relieve himself privately.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The plural 'גדרות' (fences) suggests several layers. The ברייתא learns that שאול passed through all of them and went into an inner cave. This is the first part of his צניעות.

phrases.english: It was taught: a fence within a fence,
and a cave within a cave, to relieve himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the details of the פסוק just quoted.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שאול went through several layers of fences and caves for privacy.

steps.title: שאול covered himself like a סוכה
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר reads 'להסך' as covering: even deep in the cave, שאול covered himself with his garment like a סוכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: This teaches that he covered himself like a סוכה.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר adds a second layer of צניעות. Even inside the inner cave, שאול wrapped his garment around himself like a סוכה covering.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'לְהָסֵךְ' sounds like 'סוכה' (a covering). So the פסוק hints that שאול covered himself even where no one could see. This is the צניעות that רבי אלעזר said spared שאול's life (step 16).
steps.whatToRemember: שאול's צניעות had two parts. He went deep into the cave, fence after fence and cave after cave. Even there, he covered himself like a סוכה. That modesty is what spared his life.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:
This teaches that he covered himself like a sukka.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another detail from the word 'להסך' in the same פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שאול covered himself with his garment like a סוכה, even in total privacy.

steps.title: Whoever treats clothing with contempt will not benefit from it
steps.stepSummary: On the פסוק about דוד cutting שאול's robe, רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא says that someone who disrespects clothing will end up not benefiting from clothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And דוד got up and secretly cut off the corner of שאול's robe.' רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא said: Whoever disrespects clothing will in the end not benefit from them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next פסוק in the story, where דוד cut שאול's robe. רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא learns a lesson from it about disrespecting clothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Cutting a garment is treating it with contempt. The lesson is מדה כנגד מדה (measure for measure): someone who damages clothes will later find that clothes do not help him. The proof comes in the next step.

phrases.english: 'Then David arose and cut off the corner'
of Saul's robe secretly,'
phrases.notes: שמואל א כד:ד

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina said:
Anyone who treats clothing with contempt,
in the end will not benefit from them,

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא: כׇּל הַמְבַזֶּה אֶת הַבְּגָדִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the cave story with the next פסוק but teaches a new lesson.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who disrespects clothing will eventually not benefit from clothing.

steps.title: Proof: old דוד could not get warm from clothes
steps.stepSummary: The proof is that in his old age דוד was covered with clothes but still could not get warm.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'King דוד was old, advanced in years; they covered him with clothes, but he could not get warm.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק from מלכים א to prove רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא's lesson. דוד's punishment was that clothes did not warm him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דוד cut a garment, and later garments failed him. This matches the rule from step 21: the sin and the punishment are in the same area.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is said (introduces a proof פסוק)
And he did not get warm

phrases.english: as it is stated: 'Now King David was old, advanced in years,'
and they covered him with clothes, but he could get no heat.'
phrases.notes: מלכים א א:א

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the proof for step 21.
steps.raayaObject: That disrespecting clothing leads to not benefiting from clothing.
steps.raayaSupportSource: מלכים א א:א, where old דוד could not be warmed by clothes.

steps.title: ה׳ objects to being called a מסית
steps.stepSummary: On דוד's words 'If ה׳ incited you against me', רבי אלעזר says הקדוש ברוך הוא told דוד: 'You call Me an inciter? I will make you stumble in something even schoolchildren know.'
steps.simpleTranslation: 'If ה׳ has incited you against me, let Him accept an offering.' רבי אלעזר said: הקדוש ברוך הוא said to דוד: You call Me a מסית? I will make you stumble in something that even young schoolchildren know.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes another thing דוד said to שאול. רבי אלעזר explains that ה׳ was unhappy that דוד described Him as a מסית (inciter), and promised a fitting punishment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דוד suggested that ה׳ was stirring שאול up against him. ה׳ answered מדה כנגד מדה: since דוד spoke of ה׳ as inciting, דוד himself would be 'incited' into a basic mistake. The next steps reveal what that mistake was.

keyTerms.meaning: An inciter, one who leads others astray

phrases.english: 'If the Lord has incited you against me, let Him accept an offering,'
phrases.notes: שמואל א כו:יט

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לֵיהּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְדָוִד:
phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to David:
You call Me an 'inciter'?
I will cause you to stumble in a matter

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ תִּינוֹקוֹת שֶׁל בֵּית רַבָּן יוֹדְעִים אוֹתוֹ.
phrases.english: that even schoolchildren know.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: אָמַר לֵיהּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְדָוִד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to another statement of דוד to שאול and draws a new lesson.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Because דוד called ה׳ a מסית, ה׳ caused him to stumble in a simple matter.

steps.title: The simple matter: counting ישראל requires a כופר
steps.stepSummary: The 'simple matter' is the פסוק in the Torah that counting ישראל must be done with a כופר payment.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'When you count the heads of the people of ישראל, each man shall give a ransom for his soul.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא identifies the basic thing even children know. The Torah says that when you count ישראל, each person must give a כופר (ransom), the half-shekel.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This פסוק from כי תשא is learned by young children, so it really is 'something even schoolchildren know'. Counting without the כופר brings a plague, which sets up דוד's mistake.

keyTerms.meaning: When you count (literally, 'lift up the head')
A ransom for his soul (the half-shekel)

phrases.english: As it is written: 'When you take the sum'
of the children of Israel according to their number,
then every man shall give a ransom for his soul, etc.'
phrases.notes: שמות ל:יב

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Identifies the 'simple matter' mentioned in step 23.
steps.raayaObject: That the matter is something basic that schoolchildren know.
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמות ל:יב, the law of counting with a כופר.

steps.title: ה׳ incited דוד to count ישראל
steps.stepSummary: Right away, the פסוקים say the שטן stood against ישראל and דוד was 'incited' to count ישראל. This is מדה כנגד מדה for calling ה׳ a מסית.
steps.simpleTranslation: Immediately: 'The שטן stood up against ישראל.' And it is written: 'He incited דוד against them, saying: Go, count ישראל.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the punishment came at once. דוד was incited to count the people, the very kind of inciting he had spoken of.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'וַיָּסֶת' (He incited) uses the same root as 'הסיתך' in דוד's words. That shared word is the proof of מדה כנגד מדה: דוד spoke of ה׳ inciting, so ה׳ incited him.
steps.confusionAlert: Two different פסוקים are quoted here. One (דברי הימים) says the שטן incited דוד. The other (שמואל ב) says 'He' incited דוד. The גמרא quotes the second because its word 'ויסת' matches 'הסיתך' exactly.

phrases.english: Immediately, 'Satan stood up against Israel,'
phrases.notes: דברי הימים א כא:א

phrases.english: and it is written: 'And He incited David against them,'
saying: Go, count Israel.'
phrases.notes: שמואל ב כד:א

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the fulfillment of ה׳'s warning from step 23.
steps.raayaObject: That דוד was punished measure for measure by being 'incited'.
steps.raayaSupportSource: דברי הימים א כא:א and שמואל ב כד:א

steps.title: דוד counted without a כופר, and a plague came
steps.stepSummary: When דוד counted the people he did not collect a כופר, so a plague struck ישראל 'from morning until the appointed time'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And since he counted them, he did not take a ransom from them, as it is written: 'ה׳ sent a plague on ישראל from the morning until the appointed time.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the story. דוד made exactly the simple mistake (counting without a כופר), and the result was a plague.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This closes the loop from step 23: the 'stumbling' was forgetting the כופר, which the Torah warned would bring a plague. The phrase 'עת מועד' at the end leads to the next question.
steps.whatToRemember: דוד called ה׳ a מסית, so ה׳ 'incited' him to count ישראל. He forgot the כופר, which even children know about, and a plague followed. This is מדה כנגד מדה.

phrases.english: And when he counted them
he did not take a ransom from them.
As it is written: 'So the Lord sent a pestilence upon Israel'
from the morning until the appointed time.'
phrases.notes: שמואל ב כד:טו

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵיוָן דִּמְנִינְהוּ לָא שְׁקַל מִינַּיְיהוּ כּוֹפֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the story of the census and states the punishment.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: דוד counted ישראל without a כופר, and a plague resulted.

steps.title: What does 'the appointed time' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what 'עת מועד' in the פסוק means.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is 'the appointed time'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks about a word from the פסוק it just quoted. This sets up two answers about how long the plague lasted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק does not say clearly when the plague stopped. The גמרא wants to pin down the exact ending time.

phrases.english: What is 'the appointed time'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks to define a phrase in the פסוק from step 26.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of 'עת מועד', meaning when the plague ended.

steps.title: From slaughtering the תמיד until sprinkling its blood
steps.stepSummary: שמואל סבא, in the name of רבי חנינא, says the plague lasted from the שחיטה of the תמיד until the זריקה of its blood, a very short time.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל סבא, son-in-law of רבי חנינא, said in the name of רבי חנינא: from the time the תמיד is slaughtered until its blood is sprinkled.
steps.whatsHappening: The first answer says 'עת מועד' was a short time on the same morning. It was the gap between slaughtering the morning קרבן תמיד and sprinkling its blood.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By this view, the plague started in the morning and ended very quickly. 'מועד' is understood as connected to the set time of the קרבן.

keyTerms.meaning: The slaughtering of the daily offering

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל סָבָא חַתְנֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא
phrases.english: Shmuel the elder, son-in-law of Rabbi Ḥanina, said
phrases.notes: Some read חתניה as 'father-in-law,' but the word usually means son-in-law.

phrases.english: in the name of Rabbi Ḥanina:
from the time the daily offering is slaughtered
until the time its blood is sprinkled.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל סָבָא חַתְנֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first answer to the question in step 27.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The plague lasted from the שחיטה of the תמיד until the זריקה of its blood.

steps.title: Until exactly midday
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן disagrees: 'עת מועד' means the plague lasted until exactly חצות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: Until exactly midday.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives a different answer. The plague lasted from morning until exactly חצות (noon).
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a longer time than in step 28. The two views disagree about how long the plague lasted, but both agree that it ended before the day was over.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
Until precisely midday.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמַר: עַד חֲצוֹת מַמָּשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a competing answer to the same question as step 28.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The plague lasted until exactly חצות.

steps.title: ה׳ tells the angel to take one great person, and אבישי dies
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר reads the word 'רב' in the פסוק as 'a great man.' ה׳ told the angel to take one great person whose death would pay off many of ישראל's debts. At that moment אבישי בן צרויה, equal to most of the סנהדרין, died.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'And He said to the destroying angel among the people: רב.' רבי אלעזר said: הקדוש ברוך הוא said to the angel: Take for Me the great one among them, whose death can pay off many of their debts. At that moment אבישי בן צרויה died, a man who was equal to most of the סנהדרין.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next פסוק in the plague story, and רבי אלעזר explains the word 'רב' in a new way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Simply read, 'רב' means 'enough,' telling the angel to stop. רבי אלעזר reads it as 'a great man': instead of killing many more people, the angel should take one great person. The death of a צדיק like אבישי brings atonement for the whole nation, so the plague could end.

keyTerms.meaning: The destroying angel who brought the plague
Here read as 'a great one' (not only 'enough')
To pay off debts, meaning to atone for sins
דוד's nephew and general, a great תלמיד חכם
Equal in value to the majority of the סנהדרין

steps.whyThisMatters: It teaches the idea, found in many places, that the death of a צדיק brings atonement for the generation.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not read 'רב' here only as 'enough.' רבי אלעזר's whole point is that 'רב' means 'a great man.'

phrases.english: 'And He said to the destroying angel among the people: rav.'
phrases.notes: שמואל ב כד:טז

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְמַלְאָךְ:
phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to the angel:
Take for Me the great one among them,
phrases.notes: 'רב' read as 'great one'

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ לִיפָּרַע מֵהֶם כַּמָּה חוֹבוֹת.
phrases.english: through whom many of their debts can be paid off.
phrases.notes: His death atones for many sins

phrases.aramaic: בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה מֵת אֲבִישַׁי בֶּן צְרוּיָה,
phrases.english: At that moment Avishai ben Tzeruya died,
who was equal to the majority of the Sanhedrin.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the plague story by explaining how it came to an end.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'רב' means a great man; ה׳ took אבישי בן צרויה, whose death atoned for ישראל.

steps.title: What did ה׳ see that made Him stop the plague?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a parallel פסוק that says ה׳ 'saw' and regretted the destruction, and asks what exactly He saw.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'As he was destroying, ה׳ saw and regretted.' What did He see?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a question about a word in the פסוק. This sets up four different answers that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says ה׳ 'saw' but does not say what He saw. Since ה׳ sees everything, the word must point to something specific that brought mercy. The next steps give four possible answers.

keyTerms.meaning: And He regretted (relented from the punishment)

phrases.english: 'And as he was destroying, the Lord saw and regretted,'
phrases.notes: דברי הימים א כא:טו

phrases.english: What did He see?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a parallel פסוק about the end of the plague and asks about its wording.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What did ה׳ 'see' that made Him stop the plague?

steps.title: רב: ה׳ saw יעקב אבינו
steps.stepSummary: רב says ה׳ saw יעקב אבינו, because the word 'ראה' is used about יעקב.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: He saw יעקב אבינו, as it is written: 'And יעקב said when he saw them.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב gives the first answer: ה׳ remembered יעקב אבינו and had mercy on his children.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב links the word 'ראה' in our פסוק to the same word used about יעקב. The merit of יעקב protected his descendants and stopped the plague.

phrases.english: Rav said: He saw our father Jacob,
as it is written: 'And Jacob said when he saw them.'
phrases.notes: The word 'ראה' connects the two פסוקים

steps.relationToPreviousStep: First answer to the question of step 31.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ה׳ saw the merit of יעקב אבינו.

steps.title: שמואל: ה׳ saw the ashes of יצחק
steps.stepSummary: שמואל says ה׳ saw the ashes of יצחק, connected to the עקידה, where the word 'יראה' appears.
steps.simpleTranslation: And שמואל said: He saw the ashes of יצחק, as it says: 'God will see for Himself the lamb.'
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל gives a second answer: ה׳ remembered the עקידה of יצחק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: יצחק was ready to be a קרבן, so it is as if his ashes lie before ה׳. The word 'יראה' in the עקידה story connects to 'ראה' in our פסוק. That merit brought mercy.

keyTerms.meaning: The ashes of יצחק (as if he had been offered)
Will see for Himself the lamb (בראשית כב:ח)

steps.confusionAlert: יצחק was not actually burned. 'His ashes' means ה׳ treats his willingness at the עקידה as if he had been fully offered.

phrases.english: And Shmuel said:
He saw the ashes of Isaac,
as it is said: 'God will see for Himself the lamb.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Second answer, different from רב's.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ה׳ saw the merit of the עקידה, the 'ashes' of יצחק.

steps.title: רבי יצחק נפחא: ה׳ saw the atonement money
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק נפחא says ה׳ saw the כסף כפורים, the מחצית השקל given when ישראל were counted in the מדבר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יצחק נפחא said: He saw the atonement money, as it says: 'And you shall take the atonement money from the children of ישראל, etc.'
steps.whatsHappening: A third answer: ה׳ remembered the atonement money that ישראל gave in the time of משה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This fits the cause of the plague well. דוד counted without collecting a כופר (step 26), so ה׳ looked back at the כסף כפורים given in the מדבר. That earlier payment served as atonement for the people.

keyTerms.meaning: Atonement money, the half-shekel given at a census (שמות ל:טז)

steps.whyThisMatters: This answer matches the specific sin, counting without a כופר, with its specific fix.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha said:
He saw the atonement money,
as it is said: 'And you shall take the atonement money'
from the children of Israel, etc.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Third answer, linked to the missing כופר from step 26.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ה׳ saw the כסף כפורים given in the מדבר.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: ה׳ saw the בית המקדש
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says ה׳ saw the בית המקדש, based on the פסוק 'בהר ה׳ יראה.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: He saw the בית המקדש, as it is written: 'On the mountain of ה׳ He will be seen.'
steps.whatsHappening: The fourth answer: ה׳ saw the future בית המקדש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'בהר ה׳ יראה' points to the mountain of the בית המקדש, and it uses the word 'ראה.' The plague stopped at the place where the בית המקדש would be built, and its קרבנות would bring atonement.

keyTerms.meaning: On the mountain of ה׳ He will be seen (בראשית כב:יד)

steps.whatToRemember: ה׳ 'saw' and stopped the plague. רב: יעקב. שמואל: the ashes of יצחק. רבי יצחק נפחא: the כסף כפורים. רבי יוחנן: the בית המקדש. All four play on the word 'ראה.'

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
He saw the Temple,
as it is written: 'On the mountain of the Lord He will be seen.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Fourth and final answer to the question of step 31.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ה׳ saw the future בית המקדש on that mountain.

steps.title: Two more אמוראים argue about what ה׳ saw
steps.stepSummary: רבי יעקב בר אידי and רבי שמואל בר נחמני argue. One says ה׳ saw the כסף כפורים, and the other says He saw the בית המקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יעקב בר אידי and רבי שמואל בר נחמני disagree about this. One says ה׳ saw the atonement money, and the other says He saw the בית המקדש.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings one more pair of opinions on the same question: what did ה׳ 'see' that made Him stop the plague?
steps.deeperAnalysis: These two answers are not new. They repeat the views of רבי יצחק נפחא (כסף כפורים) and רבי יוחנן (בית המקדש) from the earlier steps. Bringing back these two options sets up the next step, where the גמרא decides between them.

keyTerms.meaning: One said... and the other said (we don't know which אמורא said which)
The atonement money, meaning the half-shekel

phrases.aramaic: פְּלִיגִי בָּהּ רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב בַּר אִידֵּי
phrases.english: Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi disagrees about it
with Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani.
One said: He saw the atonement money,
phrases.notes: The מחצית השקל given when בני ישראל were counted

phrases.english: and one said: He saw the Temple.

steps.triggerLanguage: פְּלִיגִי בָּהּ רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב בַּר אִידֵּי וְרַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another dispute that narrows the earlier list down to two main options
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What did ה׳ see that made Him regret the destruction?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Either the כסף כפורים or the בית המקדש

steps.title: The גמרא sides with 'He saw the בית המקדש'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the view that ה׳ saw the בית המקדש makes the most sense. It proves this from the פסוק 'בהר ה׳ יראה'.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense to follow the one who says ה׳ saw the בית המקדש, as it says: 'As it is said to this day: On the mountain of ה׳ He will be seen.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא picks a winner. The best answer is that ה׳ saw the place of the בית המקדש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק from the עקידה links the word 'see' (יראה) to 'the mountain of ה׳,' which is the place of the future בית המקדש. The plague in דוד's time stopped at that same mountain, so the word 'saw' fits the בית המקדש best.

keyTerms.meaning: And it makes sense, it is logical
On the mountain of ה׳ He will be seen (בראשית כב:יד)

steps.whatToRemember: Of all the answers, the גמרא concludes that ה׳ 'saw' the בית המקדש. The source is 'בהר ה׳ יראה,' the mountain of the עקידה.

phrases.english: And it stands to reason like the one who says
He saw the Temple,
as it is stated: "As it is said to this day:
On the mountain of the Lord He will be seen."

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִסְתַּבְּרָא כְּמַאן דְּאָמַר בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ רָאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides between the two options in Step 36
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: ה׳ saw the בית המקדש, proven from 'בהר ה׳ יראה'

steps.title: What does 'קפנדריא' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to the משנה about respect for הר הבית and asks what the word קפנדריא means.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'A person may not enter הר הבית with his staff, etc.' What is a קפנדריא?
steps.whatsHappening: This is a new section. The גמרא quotes the משנה's list of things you may not do on הר הבית and asks about one unclear word: קפנדריא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says you may not make הר הבית into a קפנדריא, but it does not explain the word. Before learning the rule, we need to know what is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: A shortcut, passing through a place just to get somewhere else

phrases.english: A person may not enter the Temple Mount
phrases.notes: Quoting the משנה

phrases.english: with his staff, etc.
What is a "kappandarya"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the אגדה and returns to the משנה's laws about הר הבית
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of the word קפנדריא

steps.title: רבא: It means what it sounds like, a shortcut
steps.stepSummary: רבא says קפנדריא means just what its name suggests: a shortcut.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: קפנדריא means what its name says.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers simply that the word means a shortcut, the way people already use it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא treats קפנדריא as a familiar word for a short path. It needs no breakdown. Making הר הבית a shortcut means walking through it just to save steps.

keyTerms.meaning: As its name, meaning what it plainly says

phrases.english: Rava said: Kappandarya, as its name implies (a shortcut).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 38

steps.title: קפנדריא as a word-play: 'Instead of going around, I'll go through'
steps.stepSummary: רב סמא בריה דרב מרי explains the word as a combination of Aramaic words: 'Instead of going around the rows of houses, I will go in through this one.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חנא בר אדא said in the name of רב סמא son of רב מרי: It is like a person who says, 'Instead of going around the rows of houses, I'll go in through this one.'
steps.whatsHappening: A second explanation breaks the word קפנדריא into parts, like an acronym.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the word itself is built from the phrase 'אדמקיפנא אדרי, איעול בהא.' The sounds of קפנדריא come from 'מקיפנא' (going around) and 'אדרי' (rows). The meaning is still a shortcut. This step only shows where the word comes from.

keyTerms.meaning: I will go in through this one

steps.confusionAlert: רבא and רב סמא do not argue about the meaning. Both agree it means a shortcut. They differ only on how to explain the word.

phrases.english: And Rav Ḥana bar Adda

phrases.aramaic: מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב סַמָּא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב מָרִי אָמַר:
phrases.english: said in the name of Rav Sama, son of Rav Mari:
It is like a person who says:
"Instead of going around the rows of houses,
I will go in through this one."

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּמַאן דְּאָמַר אִינָשׁ: ״אַדְּמַקֵּיפְנָא אַדָּרֵי, אֵיעוּל בְּהָא״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second explanation of the word, next to רבא's
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: קפנדריא is a short form of 'I'll cut through instead of going around'

steps.title: A shortcut is allowed if you did not enter to take one
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר אבוה says the shortcut ban also applies to a בית הכנסת. But if someone entered for another reason, he may then leave through the other side.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said in the name of רבה בר אבוה: Someone who enters a בית הכנסת without planning to use it as a shortcut may then use it as a shortcut.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא carries the shortcut rule over to a בית הכנסת and gives the first case where it is allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem is entering a holy place only to cut through. If your reason for entering was proper, walking out the other side afterward is not a lack of respect.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ:
phrases.english: Rav Naḥman said that Rabba bar Avuh said:
One who enters a synagogue
not intending to make it a shortcut —
is permitted to make it a shortcut.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַנִּכְנָס לְבֵית הַכְּנֶסֶת עַל מְנָת שֶׁלֹּא לַעֲשׂוֹתוֹ קַפֶּנְדַּרְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defining the term, applies the rule to a בית הכנסת and gives an exception
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If you entered a בית הכנסת without planning a shortcut, you may then pass through

steps.title: If there was a path there first, passing through is allowed
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו says that if a public path existed before the בית הכנסת was built, people may still walk through.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו said: If it was a path from the start, it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: A second case where a shortcut through a בית הכנסת is allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The public already had the right to walk on that path. Building a בית הכנסת on top of it does not cancel that right, so walking through is not disrespect.

phrases.english: Rabbi Abbahu said:
If it was originally a path — it is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second case where a shortcut is allowed
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A path that existed before the בית הכנסת may still be used

steps.title: One who came to pray may exit through the other side
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא says someone who entered a בית הכנסת to daven may pass through it. The proof is יחזקאל's description of entering by one gate and leaving by the opposite gate.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חלבו said in the name of רב הונא: Someone who enters a בית הכנסת to daven may use it as a shortcut, as it says: 'When the people of the land come before ה׳ on the festivals...' (and they enter by one gate and leave by the opposite gate).
steps.whatsHappening: A third case where a shortcut is allowed, this time backed by a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in יחזקאל tells people coming to the מקדש on the holidays to enter through one gate and leave through the opposite one. Passing all the way through is part of honorable worship. So once you came to daven, leaving out the other side is fine.

keyTerms.meaning: Here: the ordinary people of the land (not the insult meaning)

steps.whatToRemember: Making a בית הכנסת a shortcut is forbidden, but it is allowed in three cases. (1) You entered for another reason. (2) A path was there first. (3) You came to daven.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי חֶלְבּוֹ אָמַר רַב הוּנָא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥelbo said that Rav Huna said:
One who enters a synagogue to pray
is permitted to make it a shortcut.
As it is stated: "And when the people of the land come
before the Lord on the festivals, etc."
phrases.notes: The rest of the פסוק: one who enters by the north gate leaves by the south gate (יחזקאל מו:ט)

steps.triggerLanguage: הַנִּכְנָס לְבֵית הַכְּנֶסֶת לְהִתְפַּלֵּל, מוּתָּר לַעֲשׂוֹתוֹ קַפֶּנְדַּרְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a third case where a shortcut is allowed, with a source from a פסוק
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who came to daven may pass through the בית הכנסת
steps.raayaSupportSource: יחזקאל מו:ט: enter by one gate, leave by the opposite gate

steps.title: Spitting on הר הבית is like spitting in ה׳'s eye, even today
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה that spitting on הר הבית is forbidden through a קל וחומר. רבי יהושע בן לוי adds that this still applies today and is like spitting in the pupil of ה׳'s eye.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said spitting is forbidden through a קל וחומר. רב ביבי said in the name of רבי יהושע בן לוי: Anyone who spits on הר הבית nowadays is as if he spat into the pupil of His eye, as it says: 'And My eyes and My heart will be there all the days.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next part of the משנה about spitting, then brings a strong statement showing how serious it is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's קל וחומר: if wearing shoes on הר הבית is forbidden, and shoes are not disgusting, then spitting, which is disgusting, is surely forbidden. רבי יהושע בן לוי adds that the holiness remains even without the בית המקדש. The פסוק says ה׳'s 'eyes' are there 'all the days,' meaning forever.

keyTerms.meaning: An argument from a lighter case to a stricter case (a fortiori)
Nowadays, when there is no בית המקדש

steps.whyThisMatters: It teaches that the holiness of הר הבית did not end with the חורבן. Respect for that place still applies today.

phrases.english: And spitting is forbidden through an a fortiori argument.
phrases.notes: Quoting the משנה

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב בִּיבִי אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי:
phrases.english: Rav Beivai said that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל הָרוֹקֵק בְּהַר הַבַּיִת בַּזְּמַן הַזֶּה,
phrases.english: Anyone who spits on the Temple Mount nowadays
is as if he spat into the pupil of His eye,
as it is stated: "And My eyes and My heart shall be there
all the days."
phrases.notes: מלכים א ט:ג

steps.triggerLanguage: כׇּל הָרוֹקֵק בְּהַר הַבַּיִת בַּזְּמַן הַזֶּה, כְּאִילּוּ רוֹקֵק בְּבַת עֵינוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next phrase of the משנה (spitting) after finishing קפנדריא
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Spitting on הר הבית is forbidden even today and is extremely disrespectful
steps.raayaSupportSource: 'והיו עיני ולבי שם כל הימים' (מלכים א ט:ג)

steps.title: רבא: Spitting in a בית הכנסת is permitted, like wearing shoes
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that spitting is allowed in a בית הכנסת. Spitting follows the same pattern as shoes: banned on הר הבית, allowed in a בית הכנסת.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Spitting in a בית הכנסת is permitted. It is just like the case of shoes. Shoes are forbidden on הר הבית but permitted in a בית הכנסת. Spitting is the same: it is forbidden on הר הבית but permitted in a בית הכנסת.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a new ruling. Spitting is permitted in a בית הכנסת, because spitting is modeled on wearing shoes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 44 taught that the ban on spitting on הר הבית comes from a קל וחומר from shoes. רבא reasons that a rule built on shoes should go only as far as shoes go. Shoes are allowed in a בית הכנסת, so spitting is allowed there too.

keyTerms.meaning: Just like the case of (a comparison formula)

phrases.english: Rava said:
Spitting in a synagogue is permitted,
just as in the case of a shoe.
Just as a shoe is forbidden on the Temple Mount,
but permitted in a synagogue,

phrases.aramaic: אַף רְקִיקָה, בְּהַר הַבַּיִת הוּא דְּאָסוּר,
phrases.english: so too spitting: it is on the Temple Mount that it is forbidden,
but in a synagogue it is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: רְקִיקָה בְּבֵית הַכְּנֶסֶת — שַׁרְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the spitting rule for הר הבית from step 44 and asks how it applies to a בית הכנסת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Spitting is permitted in a בית הכנסת, just as shoes are.

steps.title: Why not compare spitting to taking a shortcut instead?
steps.stepSummary: An אמורא (the name is disputed) challenges רבא: compare spitting to the shortcut ban, which applies in a בית הכנסת too.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said to רבא (some say it was רבינא, and some say רב אדא בר מתנא): Instead of learning from shoes, learn from the shortcut!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא is challenged. Why pick shoes as the model for spitting? Why not pick the shortcut ban?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 41 taught that taking a shortcut is banned in a בית הכנסת, just as on הר הבית. If spitting were modeled on the shortcut, it would be forbidden in a בית הכנסת too. That would flip רבא's ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: And some say (introduces a different version of who said it)

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said to Rava,
and some say Ravina said to Rava,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ רַב אַדָּא בַּר מַתְנָא לְרָבָא:
phrases.english: and some say Rav Adda bar Mattana said to Rava:
Instead of deriving it from a shoe,
derive it from a shortcut!
phrases.notes: The shortcut ban applies even in a בית הכנסת (step 41), so spitting would be forbidden there.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבא's choice of shoes as the model.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's ruling that spitting is permitted in a בית הכנסת
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The shortcut is also a הר הבית rule, and it carries over to a בית הכנסת. Choosing it as the model would make spitting forbidden in a בית הכנסת.

steps.title: רבא: The תנא himself learned spitting from shoes
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that the תנא of the ברייתא already chose shoes as the source. We cannot replace it with the shortcut.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: The תנא learns it from shoes, and you say to learn it from the shortcut?!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא defends his ruling. He did not pick shoes on his own. The ברייתא itself builds the spitting rule from shoes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The source of a law sets its limits. The ברייתא made spitting depend on shoes, so spitting follows the rules of shoes and not the rules of shortcuts.

keyTerms.meaning: The teacher of the ברייתא or משנה
And you say?! (expresses surprise at the other view)

phrases.english: He said to him:
The tanna derives it from a shoe,
and you say from a shortcut?!

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנָּא יָלֵיף מִמִּנְעָל, וְאַתְּ אָמְרַתְּ מִקַּפֶּנְדַּרְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 46.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Appeal to the source the תנא actually used
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any similar הר הבית rule could serve as the model for spitting, including the shortcut.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא tied spitting to shoes, so spitting follows the shoe rule and is permitted in a בית הכנסת.

steps.title: The ברייתא: Rules for entering הר הבית and the shoe קל וחומר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the ברייתא that lists what may not be brought onto הר הבית. It then derives the spitting ban through a קל וחומר from shoes.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is this source? As it was taught in a ברייתא: A person may not enter הר הבית with his staff in his hand, with his shoes on his feet, with money tied in his cloth, or with his money-belt slung behind him. He also may not use it as a shortcut. Spitting is forbidden through a קל וחומר from shoes. Wearing a shoe is not disrespectful, yet the Torah said, 'Take your shoes off your feet.' Spitting is disrespectful, so surely it is forbidden!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows the ברייתא that רבא was referring to. It proves that the spitting rule really was built on shoes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The shortcut also appears in this list, but the קל וחומר for spitting is drawn only from shoes. That supports רבא: the spitting rule depends on shoes alone. The קל וחומר runs from a non-disrespectful act (shoes) to a disrespectful one (spitting).

keyTerms.meaning: What is it? (asks for the source)

steps.confusionAlert: This is the same teaching mentioned in step 44, now quoted in full. Here its job is different: it proves that the תנא's model for spitting was shoes, not the shortcut.

phrases.english: What is it? As it was taught in a baraita:
A person may not enter the Temple Mount
not with his staff in his hand,
nor with his shoes on his feet,
nor with money tied in his cloth,
and with his money-belt slung behind him,
nor may he make it a shortcut.
And spitting is forbidden by an a fortiori argument from a shoe:

phrases.aramaic: וּמָה מִנְעָל, שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ דֶּרֶךְ בִּזָּיוֹן,
phrases.english: Just as with a shoe, which is not disrespectful,
the Torah said: 'Remove your shoes from your feet' (Exodus 3:5),
spitting, which is disrespectful,
is it not all the more so?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the ברייתא that רבא cited in step 47.
steps.raayaObject: That the spitting ban is derived specifically from shoes
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא about entering הר הבית, with the verse 'שַׁל נְעָלֶיךָ' (שמות ג:ה)

steps.title: רבי יוסי בר יהודה: A different קל וחומר from sackcloth
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי בר יהודה says the shoe proof is not needed. He derives the spitting ban from the verse in אסתר: no one may enter the king's gate wearing sackcloth.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי בר יהודה says: That proof is not needed. The verse says, 'For one may not enter the king's gate wearing sackcloth.' This is a קל וחומר. Sackcloth is not disgusting, yet before a human king it is not allowed. Spitting is disgusting, so before the King of all kings, surely it is not allowed!
steps.whatsHappening: A second תנא gives a different source for the spitting ban. He uses a verse about a human king instead of the shoe verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי בר יהודה builds a קל וחומר in two ways at once: from not disgusting (sackcloth) to disgusting (spitting), and from a human king to ה׳. This gives a second path to the same ban, without relying on shoes.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not needed (this proof is unnecessary)
Flesh and blood, a human being
The King of kings of kings (ה׳)

steps.whatToRemember: Spitting on הר הבית is forbidden. רבא rules it is permitted in a בית הכנסת, because the ברייתא learned spitting from shoes, and shoes are allowed in a בית הכנסת. רבי יוסי בר יהודה reaches the spitting ban another way, through sackcloth before a king.
steps.whyThisMatters: The source chosen for a law sets its boundaries. That is why the debate over shoes versus shortcut decides whether spitting is allowed in a בית הכנסת.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda says:
It is not needed:
Behold, it says:
'For none may enter the king's gate
clothed in sackcloth' (Esther 4:2).
And is this matter not an a fortiori argument?
Just as sackcloth, which is not repulsive,
is treated so before flesh and blood,
spitting, which is repulsive,
before the King of kings of kings,
is it not all the more so?!

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: אֵינוֹ צָרִיךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers an alternative source to the shoe-based קל וחומר in the ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Spitting before ה׳ is forbidden through a קל וחומר from sackcloth before a human king.

steps.title: The challenger explains: be strict in both places
steps.stepSummary: The challenger tells רבא he is not replacing the shoe source. He wants to apply stringency both on הר הבית and in the בית הכנסת.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: This is what I meant. Let us be strict here, and be strict here too.
steps.whatsHappening: The challenger responds to רבא's answer from Step 47 by explaining what he really meant. He restates his challenge in a sharper form, which sets up רבא's next reply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא had said we cannot drop the shoe comparison that the תנא chose. The challenger agrees we keep it. He argues we can still be strict in both directions: the shoe comparison bans spitting on הר הבית, and the shortcut comparison bans it in the בית הכנסת. So the objection survives: why should spitting be allowed in a בית הכנסת at all?

keyTerms.meaning: This is what I meant. A speaker uses it to clarify his earlier words.
To be strict, choosing the stricter ruling

steps.confusionAlert: The challenger is not arguing against the shoe source. He accepts it for הר הבית. He wants to add the shortcut comparison so that spitting is also banned in the בית הכנסת. That is the meaning of 'strict here and strict here.'

phrases.english: He said to him: I meant the following:
phrases.notes: The challenger, רב פפא (or רבינא, or רב אדא בר מתנא), is speaking to רבא.

phrases.english: Let us say: be strict here
phrases.notes: Here means הר הבית. We keep the ban that comes from the shoe comparison.

phrases.english: and be strict here too,
phrases.notes: Here means the בית הכנסת. We ban spitting there as well, based on the shortcut comparison.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's reply in Step 47. The challenger clarifies and renews his challenge from Step 46.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's ruling in Step 45 that spitting is allowed in a בית הכנסת
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: We do not need to choose between the two comparisons. Use each one where it makes us stricter: shoes for הר הבית and the shortcut for the בית הכנסת. Then spitting would be banned in a בית הכנסת, against רבא's ruling.
